In a park in south London stands
a strange, bulky creature made
of concrete, with a horn on its nose.
More than a hundred and seventy
years ago, this was what the best
scientists of the day thought a
dinosaur looked like.
They were wrong, in many surprising ways.
Today, let's follow how pictures
of extinct animals changed,
from swamp monsters to feathered,
colorful animals, and why every
generation was so sure it had
finally got it right.
Long before paleontology existed,
people found enormous bones in
the ground and tried to explain them.
Some historians suggest that ancient
Greeks saw the bones of giant
ancient mammals as the remains
of heroes or monsters from their myths.
In China, fossil bones and teeth
were long sold as dragon bones
for traditional medicine.
The modern story begins in the
1820s in Sussex, England,
with a doctor named Gideon Mantell.
According to the traditional story,
his wife Mary Ann found some unusual
fossil teeth.
Mantell noticed that they looked
like the teeth of a modern iguana,
only much bigger.
So he imagined the animal as a
giant lizard, and in 1825 he named
it Iguanodon, meaning iguana tooth.
That simple comparison shaped the
way the animal was pictured for decades.
Among the bones Mantell later
studied was a cone-shaped spike.
He guessed that it was a horn,
and in his sketches it ended up
on the tip of the animal's nose,
like a rhinoceros.
Early pictures showed Iguanodon
as a huge four-legged lizard with
a spike on its snout.
It was a reasonable guess from
a few scattered bones.
It was also completely wrong.
The horn was finally explained
in 1878, deep in a coal mine
at Bernissart in Belgium.
Miners found dozens of Iguanodon
skeletons, many of them nearly complete.
When the scientist Louis Dollo
studied them, the mystery spike
turned up on the hand.
It was a thumb spike,
not a nose horn.
And the skeletons suggested an
animal that could rise up on its
strong hind legs, not a lizard
sprawled on four.
Before that discovery, London built
the world's first life-sized
dinosaur sculptures.
In 1854, the artist Benjamin
Waterhouse Hawkins unveiled them
in the grounds of the Crystal
Palace, working with the anatomist
Richard Owen.
Owen saw dinosaurs as advanced
reptiles with sturdy, almost
mammal-like legs, so the sculptures
look like heavy, elephant-shaped lizards.
They are still there today,
and they are now protected as
historic monuments.
Hawkins also knew how to make headlines.
On New Year's Eve,
1853, he held a dinner for
scientists and guests inside the
mold of one of his Iguanodon models.
Men in formal suits sat at a
table inside the body of a
half-finished dinosaur, eating
and making speeches.
It was a celebration of science,
even though the shape they were
celebrating would soon look very
old-fashioned.
Let's put the three versions side by side.
In 1825, Mantell named Iguanodon
from a handful of teeth and imagined
a giant iguana.
In 1854, the Crystal Palace
sculpture showed a heavy four-legged
beast with a horn on its nose.
And after the Bernissart skeletons
were found in 1878,
the horn moved to the thumb,
and the animal stood up on its hind legs.
In America, the race to find
dinosaurs turned into a bitter
feud known as the Bone Wars.
Edward Drinker Cope and Othniel
Charles Marsh competed for decades
to find and name new fossils in
the American West.
They raced each other into print,
attacked each other's work,
and were accused of bribery and
of damaging fossil sites to keep
them from the other.
In their hurry, both men made famous mistakes.
In 1869, Cope described
Elasmosaurus, a marine reptile
with an enormously long neck.
But in his reconstruction,
he put the skull on the wrong
end, at the tip of the tail.
His mentor, Joseph Leidy,
pointed out the error.
Cope tried to recall and destroy
the printed copies and published
a corrected version.
Marsh, his rival, kept bringing
up the mistake for decades.
Marsh had his own famous slip.
In 1879 he named a giant long-necked
dinosaur Brontosaurus, the thunder lizard.
Its skeleton was found without
a skull, so his reconstruction
borrowed a short, boxy skull based
on a different dinosaur, Camarasaurus.
For about a century,
museum mounts of this kind of
sauropod wore the wrong kind of head.
The longer, more slender head was
only widely accepted in the late 1970s.
Then there was Stegosaurus,
named by Marsh in 1877.
Its large, flat bony plates were
found scattered near the backbone,
so at first he thought they lay
flat along the back,
like tiles on a roof.
That is where the name comes from:
Stegosaurus means roof lizard.
Later and better skeletons showed
that the plates stood upright,
in two rows along the back.
Stegosaurus also gave rise to a famous myth.
Its brain was tiny for such a big animal.
But there was a large space in
the spine near the hips,
and Marsh suggested it might have
held a second nerve center that
helped control the back legs and tail.
The idea spread as the dinosaur
with two brains.
Today, many scientists think that
space held something else,
possibly a store of energy-rich
tissue like the one found in birds.
Around 1900, paleoart found its
first great master, the American
painter Charles R. Knight.
He studied living animals closely
and worked with scientists to bring
skeletons back to life.
His 1897 painting of two leaping
predators, known as Leaping Laelaps,
showed dinosaurs as lively, fighting animals.
His museum murals shaped how
millions pictured the prehistoric world.
But artists followed the science
of their time.
For much of the twentieth century,
many experts thought giant sauropods
like Brontosaurus and Diplodocus
were too heavy to move easily on land.
So they were often painted standing
in lakes and swamps,
with the water taking some of their
weight and only their long necks
rising above the surface.
Dinosaurs in general were seen
as slow, dim, cold-blooded animals.
Physics eventually sank that idea.
In 1951, the British scientist
Kenneth Kermack pointed out a problem.
An animal standing deep underwater
with only its head at the surface
would have water pressing hard
against its chest.
Its lungs could barely expand,
so it would struggle to breathe.
Later studies of sauropod feet,
legs and trackways also pointed
to animals that walked on dry land.
Big predators were drawn just as wrongly.
For decades, Tyrannosaurus rex
was shown standing upright,
like a giant kangaroo,
with its heavy tail resting on the ground.
Museums mounted skeletons this
way, and movie monsters copied the pose.
It looked powerful, but it did
not fit the skeleton.
To stand like that,
the animal would have had to bend
or even break its own joints.
Footprints helped settle the question.
Thousands of dinosaur trackways
have been found around the world,
and drag marks from tails are extremely rare.
If dinosaurs had dragged their
tails, the ancient mud should be
full of grooves.
Instead, the tracks show that
dinosaurs carried their tails up
off the ground, balancing the body
like a seesaw over the hips.
Mistakes were not only made with dinosaurs.
In 1909, Charles Walcott discovered
the Burgess Shale in the Canadian
Rockies, full of strange animals
more than five hundred million years old.
Many of them looked so alien that
scientists struggled to place them.
Some of the results were,
looking back, very funny.
Take Anomalocaris.
Its spiny front appendages were
first described as the bodies of
a kind of shrimp.
Its round mouth, with plates
arranged in a ring,
was named as a jellyfish called Peytoia.
And a crushed body fossil was
treated as a sea cucumber.
For decades, these pieces were
described as separate animals.
In the 1980s, the paleontologists
Harry Whittington and Derek Briggs
showed that these pieces belonged together.
Whittington found one of the
shrimp-like appendages still
attached near the mouth.
The parts formed a single animal:
a swimming predator with large
eyes, flaps along its body and
two grasping front limbs.
It was one of the largest animals
of its time, probably up to about
forty centimeters long.
Then there is Hallucigenia,
a tiny worm-like animal whose name
comes from the word hallucination.
In 1977, Simon Conway Morris
reconstructed it walking on seven
pairs of stiff spines,
with a row of soft tentacles waving
from its back.
Scientists wondered how any animal
could walk on stiff, pointed spikes.
The answer was that it had been
drawn upside down.
In the early 1990s,
new fossils from China showed that
the spines were on its back,
for defense, and the soft tentacles
were really legs.
Then, in 2015, a closer study found
its real head, with eyes and a
mouth, at the other end.
The blob once taken for a head
was probably a smear of fluid from
the decaying body.
The animal had been upside down and backwards.
Back on land, the big change came
in the 1960s.
In Montana, the Yale paleontologist
John Ostrom studied a new predator
he named Deinonychus in 1969.
It was light, with a stiffened
tail for balance and a large curved
claw on each foot.
Ostrom argued that this was an
active, agile hunter, not a sluggish lizard.
His work helped start what became
known as the Dinosaur Renaissance.
Ostrom's student Robert Bakker
pushed the idea further.
He argued that dinosaurs were
warm-blooded, active animals, closer
to birds and mammals than to lizards.
He drew them running and leaping.
Many colleagues were skeptical,
and the details are still debated today.
But the old image of dinosaurs
as slow, dull reptiles started to fade.
Many people first saw this new
image in 1993, in the film Jurassic Park.
Advised by paleontologists,
including Jack Horner, the
filmmakers showed dinosaurs as
fast, alert animals, with tails
held high off the ground.
No animal shows how pictures can
change better than Spinosaurus.
In 1912, fossils of a huge predator
were found in the Egyptian desert,
and the German paleontologist Ernst
Stromer described them in 1915.
The animal had long jaws and spines
on its back at least one point
six five meters long,
which seemed to hold up a large sail.
Stromer's fossils were kept in
a museum in Munich.
Stromer was a critic of the Nazi
regime, and tension with the
museum's Nazi director meant the
fossils were not moved to safety.
On the night of the twenty-fourth
to the twenty-fifth of April,
1944, Allied bombs hit the museum,
and the Spinosaurus fossils were destroyed.
Only Stromer's drawings and
descriptions remained.
For decades, Spinosaurus was known
mostly from those drawings and
a few scraps.
Artists often gave it the body
of a typical large two-legged
predator, added a sail on its back
and a long, crocodile-like snout.
In the 2001 film Jurassic Park
Three, it was shown defeating a Tyrannosaurus.
To many fans, it became the greatest
land predator of all.
Then new fossils from Morocco
changed the picture.
In 2014, a team led by Nizar
Ibrahim described a partial skeleton
with surprisingly short hind legs
and dense bones.
They proposed that Spinosaurus
spent much of its life in rivers,
catching fish.
Some other scientists disputed
parts of this reconstruction,
and the argument was only beginning.
In 2020, the same team described its tail.
It was tall and flat,
with long spines forming something
like a fin, a bit like the
tail of a newt.
They argued it could push the animal
through water.
Other researchers have since argued
that Spinosaurus waded in shallow
water more like a heron,
or was a slow surface swimmer.
The debate continues, and that
is exactly the point:
the picture is still changing.
In just over a century,
Spinosaurus has been redrawn again and again.
In 1915, Stromer described a giant
predator with a sail.
In 1944, the original fossils were
lost in the war.
In 2014, new fossils gave it short
hind legs and a life in the water.
And in 2020, a paddle-like tail
made it look more like a swimmer than ever.
Scientists are still arguing about
how it really lived.
Another habit in paleoart was what
artists call shrink-wrapping.
Many restorations were made by
drawing a skeleton and then
stretching a thin layer of skin
tightly over it.
Every opening in the skull and
every bump of bone showed through.
The animals looked starved,
with no fat, no muscle bulk and
no soft tissue.
In 2012, the paleoartists John
Conway and C. M. Kosemen,
with the paleontologist Darren
Naish, published a book called All Yesterdays.
To show the problem,
they drew living animals the same
shrink-wrapped way, using only
their skeletons.
A swan or a cat drawn like
this looked like a strange, bony monster.
Future scientists, they suggested,
would get our animals very wrong
if they used our old methods.
That brings up a question that
is still argued about:
did big predatory dinosaurs have lips?
Movies usually show rows of bare
teeth, like a crocodile.
But a 2023 study compared tooth
wear and skull shapes,
and concluded that many theropods,
including Tyrannosaurus, probably
had lips that covered their teeth
when the mouth was closed,
more like a monitor lizard.
The biggest visual change came
from northeastern China.
In 1996, a farmer in Liaoning
Province found Sinosauropteryx,
a small predatory dinosaur with
a fringe of simple,
hair-like filaments along its back and tail.
It was the first non-bird dinosaur
found with feather-like coverings.
In the years that followed,
many more feathered dinosaurs came
out of the same rocks.
The scaly, lizard-like raptors
of nineties films soon looked outdated.
In 2007, scientists found quill
knobs on the forearm bone of a Velociraptor.
In living birds, these small bumps
anchor large wing feathers.
So Velociraptor almost certainly
had feathered arms.
It was not a scaly monster,
but a feathered, bird-like hunter
about the size of a turkey.
For a long time,
the colors in paleoart were pure guesswork.
Then, in 2010, researchers looked
at fossil feathers under powerful
electron microscopes.
They found tiny structures called
melanosomes, which hold pigment.
Different shapes of melanosomes
give different colors in living birds.
By comparing them, scientists could
start to estimate the real colors
of extinct animals.
Sinosauropteryx was one of the
first dinosaurs to get a color.
The 2010 study found that its tail
had alternating bands, reddish-brown
and pale, a striped tail a little
like a red panda's.
A later study, in 2017,
suggested it was darker on top
and lighter underneath, with a
dark band across the eyes,
like a bandit mask.
For the first time,
artists were painting a dinosaur's
colors from evidence.
Soon other dinosaurs followed.
Anchiornis, a small feathered
dinosaur from China, was found
to have a mostly gray and black
body, white wing feathers with
black tips, and a reddish crown
of feathers on its head.
And in 2012, a study of Microraptor
found that its black feathers
probably had a glossy,
iridescent sheen, like a modern
crow or starling.
Here is how quickly the colors arrived.
In 2010, Sinosauropteryx got a
striped, reddish-brown tail.
The same year, Anchiornis got gray,
black and white feathers with a reddish crest.
In 2012, Microraptor got glossy
black, iridescent feathers.
Within a few years,
dinosaurs went from pure guesswork
to animals with colors backed by evidence.
After these discoveries, some
artists put feathers on almost
every dinosaur, and giant
tyrannosaurs began to look like
huge, fluffy birds.
But in 2017, a study of skin
impressions from Tyrannosaurus
and its relatives found small scales
on the neck, hips and tail.
So adult Tyrannosaurus was probably
mostly scaly.
One idea is that a very large
body holds heat easily and doesn't
need an insulating coat,
though younger animals might have
been fuzzier.
Scans have also changed how we see sauropods.
Their huge neck bones were full
of air spaces, connected to a system
of air sacs similar to those of modern birds.
That made their skeletons much
lighter than they looked,
while staying strong.
Instead of heavy, swamp-bound
giants, sauropods now appear as
well-built land animals, with long
necks that could reach a wide area
of food without moving their bodies.
Another surprise came from studying
how dinosaurs grew.
By looking at bone tissue under
the microscope, scientists can
tell whether an animal was young
or fully grown.
In 2009, Jack Horner and Mark
Goodwin argued that two dome-headed
dinosaurs, Dracorex and Stygimoloch,
were really young forms of Pachycephalosaurus.
As the animals grew,
their skulls changed shape so much
that they had been given different names.
In 2010, a similar idea was proposed
for Triceratops.
Torosaurus, with its larger frill
pierced by two openings,
might be a fully grown Triceratops.
This idea is still debated,
and many paleontologists think
they were separate animals.
But it shows that some dinosaurs
may have changed dramatically as
they aged, and a single restoration
can only show one moment in an animal's life.
Look back over the last hundred
and seventy years.
We started with concrete lizards
in a London park,
with horns on their noses.
We passed through swamp-bound giants
and tail-dragging monsters.
Now we have scanned skeletons,
fossil colors and computer models.
And at every stage,
people believed they were close
to the final answer.
So what will people a hundred years
from now think of our pictures?
They may laugh at our feathers,
our lips, or our Spinosaurus.
Being willing to be proven wrong
is not a weakness of science.
It is how science works.
Mantell's horn and Cope's misplaced
head were not failures,
but first attempts.
